name: Combined oral contraceptive pill

lead: Combined oral contraceptives contain an estrogen and a progestin. Besides preventing pregnancy, some are prescribed to reduce acne and excess hair growth in women, with fewer hormonal breakouts as the payoff.

The estrogen component appears to suppress ovarian androgen production and raises sex hormone-binding globulin, which lowers free testosterone. Lower free androgens mean less sebum. Four combined pills are FDA-approved for moderate acne in people who have started menstruating and also want contraception, and studies show reductions in both inflammatory and non-inflammatory facial lesions. Progestin-only pills have not been shown to help acne.

paras: It is taken as a prescribed daily pill, chosen with a clinician for the formulation and the person's health history. Acne improvement is generally described over a few months, and it is often used alongside topical treatments.

Common effects include breakthrough bleeding, nausea, headache, breast tenderness and bloating. Venous clot risk is higher in users than non-users in absolute terms (about 60 versus 30 per 100,000 woman-years) and varies by progestin; the FDA added a warning to drospirenone pill labels in 2012. Smoking over 35, migraine with aura, and a history of clots or stroke are among the listed contraindications. It is prescription-only.

angle.text: Women use the combined pill to cut androgen activity and oil production, which leads to fewer hormonal breakouts and clearer skin. Its use for acne is studied and recognised in dermatology.

lead: The combined oral contraceptive pill (COC) is a hormonal medicine containing an estrogen and a progestin, taken mainly for contraception. It is also prescribed for acne and hirsutism in women, since lowering androgen activity reduces sebum production [1][2].

Four combined pills are FDA-approved for moderate acne in patients who are at least 14 or 15 years old, have begun menstruating, and need contraception: Ortho Tri-Cyclen, Estrostep, Beyaz and YAZ [1]. Wikipedia's acne article reports lesion reductions of roughly 40 to 70 percent with combined pills, and notes that a 2014 review found oral antibiotics somewhat better at three months but roughly equal at six months [2].

The pill is a conventional prescription treatment. In looksmaxxing and skin-care communities it is relevant mainly to women's discussions of hormonal acne; the sources reviewed for this article contain no substantial forum material about it.

paras: Combined pills are sometimes prescribed for androgen-related acne and hirsutism [1]. Wikipedia reports that third- or fourth-generation progestins, or antiandrogenic ones such as cyproterone acetate, are preferred for acne, and that first-generation progestins may worsen it [2].

The primary use is pregnancy prevention. Registered post-authorisation studies exist for specific products, for example a Phase 4 safety and efficacy study of YAZ in China that enrolled 1,921 women with contraception as the condition studied [3].

Studies cited by Wikipedia show that combined pills reduce both inflammatory and non-inflammatory facial acne lesions, whereas progestin-only pills have not been shown to be effective [1]. The acne article gives a range of about 40 to 70 percent fewer lesions and describes pills as a reasonable first-line option for some women [2].
Breakthrough bleeding is the most common effect. Nausea, vomiting, headache, bloating, breast tenderness, fluid retention and weight change may also occur [1].

The absolute risk of venous thrombosis is reported as about 60 per 100,000 woman-years in current users versus 30 in non-users, compared with 100 to 200 per 100,000 pregnant women per year [1]. Risk varies by progestin; compared with levonorgestrel, rate ratios for deep venous thrombosis are reported as 1.82 for desogestrel, 1.86 for gestodene, 1.64 for drospirenone and 1.88 for cyproterone acetate [1]. An FDA review of more than 800,000 women led to a 2012 warning on drospirenone labels [1]. Pills with more than 50 micrograms of estrogen are linked to higher ischemic stroke and heart attack risk [1].

WHO and CDC eligibility criteria list as category 4 (should not be used) conditions such as migraine with aura, a history of DVT, pulmonary embolism or stroke, smoking 15 or more cigarettes daily at age 35 or older, blood pressure of 160/100 mm Hg or higher, known thrombogenic mutations, current breast cancer and severe cirrhosis or liver tumours. Pills should not be taken during known pregnancy [1].
For acne, the estrogen component appears to suppress ovarian androgen production and raise SHBG, lowering free testosterone and therefore sebum output [1].

The first oral contraceptive was approved by the FDA and marketed in the United States in 1960. First-generation pills used high estrogen doses; later generations lowered the estrogen and varied the progestin, with third and fourth generations arriving from the 1990s [1].

Human studies cited by reference sources report reductions in acne lesions with combined pills, and a 2014 review compared them with oral antibiotics [1][2]. No specific acne trial is detailed here; the only registered study found for this entry is a post-authorisation safety and efficacy study of YAZ in Chinese women using it for contraception [3].

timeline.event: The first oral contraceptive is approved by the FDA and marketed in the United States [1].
The FDA adds a clotting-risk warning to the drospirenone pill label [1].
